reading.title: Sharpening the Final Debate Case
reading.purpose: Listen as two eighth-grade debaters stress-test their case before Saturday's tournament.
paras: "Read your opening claim again," Tessa said, tapping a yellow highlighter against her desk. "If we argue that middle school should start forty minutes later, the other team's first objection will be bus costs. How do we preempt that complaint—deal with it in advance before they even step to the podium?"

"Easy," Mateo answered, flipping to his second index card. "We include a clear caveat right after our main claim, adding a condition that the schedule shift applies only after districts stagger two existing bus routes. That way our rebuttal does not sound defensive when they raise the budget."

Tessa nodded and circled a statistic on his sheet. "Good, now look at this line about homework. Your link between start times and fewer missing papers feels tenuous, thin and weakly supported by just one small survey. Let us replace it with the three-year sleep study from the medical journal. Those numbers are indisputable—so solidly backed that no judge can brush them aside—and they will bolster our entire case."

"What about my comparison?" Mateo asked. "I used an analogy comparing an exhausted student to a phone running at two percent battery." Tessa grinned. "That image lands instantly. Just cut the phrase 'minor scheduling inconvenience' when describing a 6:00 a.m. bus stop. Calling a freezing dark sidewalk a minor inconvenience is both a polite euphemism and a huge understatement. Say plainly that students are waiting in the dark—your evidence is strong enough to speak straight."

qs.q: In paragraph 3, the word "tenuous" most nearly means
choices: backed by three years of careful medical research
thin and weakly supported by little real evidence
phrased politely to soften an unpleasant reality
stated in advance to block a rival's best question
qs.why: Tessa defines tenuous directly as "thin and weakly supported by just one small survey."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why Tessa tells Mateo to drop the phrase "minor scheduling inconvenience"?
choices: Calling a freezing dark sidewalk a minor inconvenience is both a polite euphemism and a huge understatement.
Say plainly that students are waiting in the dark—your evidence is strong enough to speak straight.
qs.why: This sentence explains that the phrase softens and shrinks a serious reality (waiting on a freezing dark sidewalk).

ev.text: Calling a freezing dark sidewalk a minor inconvenience is both a polite euphemism and a huge understatement.

qs.q: Why does Mateo add a caveat about staggering bus routes right after his opening claim?
choices: It addresses the opposing team's likely budget complaint before they can use it.
It proves that most middle school students prefer walking in the dark.
It lets the debaters avoid citing any medical studies about student sleep.
It replaces their opening claim with a humorous comparison about phones.
qs.why: In paragraphs 1 and 2, Mateo adds the condition specifically to preempt the bus-cost objection so their rebuttal is stronger.

qs.q: What is the main focus of Tessa and Mateo's rehearsal?
choices: Deciding which school district should buy brand-new buses before winter.
Strengthening a debate case by anticipating objections, upgrading evidence, and speaking plainly.
Comparing different ways to highlight index cards before a Saturday tournament.
Proving that analogies are always more convincing than three-year medical studies.
qs.why: The teammates tighten their argument by adding a caveat, replacing tenuous support with solid data, and cutting evasive phrasing.

clues.text: deal with it in advance before they even step to the podium
adding a condition that the schedule shift applies only after districts stagger two existing bus routes
so solidly backed that no judge can brush them aside
comparing an exhausted student to a phone running at two percent battery
